The Blackwood Pack: Unchosen
They put his name on a door. He wants a handle on the inside.
A lone wolf throws the pack's claim back into the alpha's truck. To keep him, Ronan has to make leaving possible.

Kai Nakoa was only passing through Blackwood territory when the pack claimed him: name in the ledger, name on a bunkhouse door that locks from the hall. Ronan Blackwood, the alpha who inherited that law from his father, has to decide whether protecting his people means keeping them or letting them go. Silas, the archivist, holds the pen and has been waiting years to use it. You decide whether belonging is something that can be given, or only something you choose.
An adult traveler whose car died on the Blackwood switchback the same night Kai threw the crest back, and who got offered a door too.
If nobody acts, the claim law stands, Kai's name stays on a door that locks from the outside, and Blackwood keeps calling a cage a home.

He threw the crest back. He kept the chain it hung on.

To choose where he belongs, out loud, with the door unlocked.

Rules straight lines with a ruler when he's furious
Brews tea nobody asked for when he's worried about someone
He guards the ledger for a living and has wanted to burn it since he was sixteen.
Footnotes, rain on the archive skylight, a clean amendment

A Name on a Door
Undo a claim Kai never agreed to
The switchback road, Ronan's truck
Tuesday, 5:40 PM
Dusk on the switchback. Kai flags down Ronan's truck, walks up to the open window, and drops a brass crest onto the passenger seat.
Your people put my name on a door.
It means you have a home.
A home has a handle on the inside.
The bunkhouse door he means locks from the hall side. Everyone in Blackwood knows it. Nobody has said it out loud in forty years.
He's right. And I've signed off on that door eleven times.
I shoulder my pack. There's a bus ticket to Missoula folded in my back pocket, and I am not asking permission to use it.
I pick up the crest. It's still warm from his hand.
What does Ronan do?
Take his name off the door tonight.
I'll take it down myself. Tonight.
Just like that? No committee? No ancient howling?
I turn the truck around. At the bunkhouse I unscrew the nameplate with my pocketknife and hand it to him through the window, screws and all.
Ronan unscrewed Kai's nameplate from the bunkhouse door that night and gave it to him.
Offer dinner. No strings, no crest.
Eat with us before you decide anything. Dinner doesn't sign you up for a thing.
And if I eat and still leave?
Then you leave fed.
I get in the truck. I keep my hand on the door handle the whole way down. He notices. He doesn't say a word about it.
Kai agreed to one no-strings dinner at the pack house; his name is still in the ledger.
Tell him the claim holds until council.
The claim stands until the council meets. That's the law. Not me.
Funny how the law always sounds exactly like you.
I walk down the mountain on foot. I don't look back, which takes more effort than it should.
I told myself I was protecting him. My hands on the wheel say otherwise.
Ronan kept the claim in place pending council; Kai walked off angry and trust took a hit.
The Ledger
Explain the danger without making Kai's choice for him
The Blackwood pack house, the long kitchen table
Wednesday, 7:15 PM
Kai is at the long table because the ledger is. Silas sets it down like it might bite and opens it to four centuries of handwriting.
Cross it out. My name. You've got a pen right there.
You'd be unprotected.
Then explain the danger. Don't make my choice for me.
The rule protects the line. Not always the person.
Unclaimed wolves east of the creek get run off by the Crane pack. That's the danger. It's real. It's still not anyone's call but yours.
Kai drags the ledger closer. Three lines above his name, Ronan's own is crossed out, then written back in, darker, in someone else's hand.
Huh. Who crossed you out, Alpha?
I did. At nineteen. With a packed bag by the door.
What does Ronan do?
Lay out the risk. Then hand Kai the pen.
Crane land starts at the creek. Stay west of it and you're fine. That's everything I know.
I put the pen in his hand and take my own hands off the table.
I'm not striking it tonight. Walk the treeline with me at dawn. You owe me the kid who crossed himself out.
Ronan explained the Crane risk and handed Kai the pen; Kai held off and asked to hear Ronan's story at dawn.
Ask Silas to draft a voluntary column first.
Silas. Can the ledger have a column for people who choose it?
It can have whatever we're brave enough to write. Give me two days.
Two days. Not three. And at dawn you tell me about that crossed-out name.
Ronan asked Silas to draft a voluntary column; Kai gave them two days and asked about Ronan's crossed-out name.
Close the ledger. Not in front of everyone.
Not at dinner. Not like this.
I open the ledger again and slide it back to Kai. I don't ask Ronan. For once, I don't ask.
You don't get to pick where I'm allowed to say no. Treeline, dawn. Come alone and bring the truth, or don't come.
Ronan shut the ledger to keep it private; Silas reopened it for Kai, who demanded the truth at the treeline at dawn.
What You Never Got To
Admit the leaving Ronan never finished
The treeline above the creek
Thursday, 6:00 AM
Fog sits on the creek. Ronan walks the treeline with his hands jammed in his jacket, like they might do something without him.
I had a bus ticket at nineteen. My father got sick the week I was supposed to go. Somebody had to hold the pack.
So you stayed out of duty.
I stayed because I was needed. That's different.
Is it? You want me to choose what you never got to.
I wanted you not to regret it.
Regret can be mine too.
I stop at the water. West bank is Blackwood. East bank is nobody's. I could step across right now, and we both know it.
What does Ronan do?
Tell him the choice is his. Mean it.
Then regret it on your own terms. I'm done deciding for you.
Say that in front of the council.
I will. Full moon. Every family.
Ronan told Kai the choice was his and promised to say so before the council at the full moon.
Give him the map. Don't ask him to stay.
I hand him the patrol map, Crane markers circled in red. I don't say stay. It's harder than lifting the truck.
No speech?
Just the map. Where you take it is yours.
Ronan gave Kai the patrol map with the danger zones marked and did not ask him to stay.
Tell him the bond already decided.
It isn't only the ledger. My wolf knew you on sight. That's a bond, Kai.
Then your wolf can learn the word no.
I step into the creek, one boot on nobody's land. This is me, deciding.
I reached for the oldest excuse there is. He deserved better from me.
Ronan invoked a fated bond to hold Kai; Kai stepped across the creek to show it didn't bind him.
The Handle on the Inside
Let Kai actually leave once, not just be told he can
The archive under the pack house
Saturday, 10:00 AM
The archive smells like cedar and old paper. Silas has drawn a new column in the ledger with a ruler, because of course he used a ruler.
I move Kai's name from Claimed to the column I've labeled Voluntary. My handwriting is steadier than I feel.
Is the road still open?
You can leave now.
I will walk with you if you want.
To the road. Not past it.
To the road.
I will record the choice, not a claim.
What does Ronan do?
Walk him to the road and stop there.
Two miles of gravel. Neither of them talks. At the county road Ronan stops exactly on the line, like it's painted.
I cross. I stand on the asphalt a full minute, just to know I can.
Road's open. It stays open.
Ronan walked Kai to the county road and stopped at the line; Kai crossed out of the territory.
Walk him there. Ask for one text.
One text when you get where you're going. Not permission. Just so I sleep.
One text. If I feel like it.
I cross with my phone in my hand. Forty minutes later I send it: Bus smells like feet. Still free.
Kai left the territory and texted Ronan once, on his own terms.
Let Silas walk him. You can't watch.
Silas walks you. I can't do the road part yet. That's mine to fix, not yours to carry.
I walk Kai to the county line. He asks if Ronan's always like this. I tell him no. He's usually worse at admitting it.
I cross. Then I look back up the hill, where one window has a very large shadow in it.
Ronan stayed behind and Silas walked Kai to the county road; Kai crossed and saw Ronan watching from a window.
His No Counts
Make the right to leave real, in front of every family
The council ring, Blackwood hollow
Full moon, 9:00 PM
Five families around the fire ring. The Harlan elders sit with their arms crossed, which in wolf is a whole paragraph.
Any adult wolf can refuse the ledger. Anyone who stays, stays because they asked to. Starting tonight.
Old Harlan stands. When the strays bring Crane trouble to our fences, he asks, who pays?
We do. His no counts. Even when it costs us.
I read the new clause aloud twice, slowly, so nobody can claim later that they misheard.
Kai doesn't thank Ronan. He walks to the east edge of the ring, where two young Harlan wolves sit like they've been waiting years for a door.
Mae. Tobin. You said you wanted out. The road's open. I'll walk you.
He isn't paying me back with a kiss. He's making me prove it. Good.
What does Ronan do?
Keep the path clear. Personally.
I stand and step between the Harlan elders and the east trail. I don't growl. I don't have to.
Mae and Tobin walk out behind Kai. Nobody stops them. It's the quietest earthquake Blackwood has ever had.
Ronan physically kept the east trail clear while Kai walked Mae and Tobin out of the territory.
Pass it tonight. Hear objections in writing.
It passes tonight. Any family can object in writing, and Silas will answer every word.
In writing. With citations. I've been waiting eleven years for this.
I walk Mae and Tobin out anyway. The law can catch up with its paperwork.
The exit right passed with a written-objection period; Kai walked Mae and Tobin out that night.
Free Blackwood's wolves only. Don't force the Harlans.
I can't rule the Harlans. I can rule Blackwood. Our ledger is voluntary as of now.
The Harlan elders leave with Mae and Tobin in tow. Mae looks back at Kai the whole way down the hill.
Half a law. Better than none. Worse than you think.
Ronan made only Blackwood's ledger voluntary; the Harlans refused and took Mae and Tobin home.
My Own Key
Agree on a trial stay, and a key that's Kai's
Ronan's front porch
One week later, Sunday, 8:30 PM
A knock. Not the pack knock, three short raps. Just one. And then waiting.
I open the door. Kai is on the porch with his own duffel, his own map, and the face of a man who rehearsed this in a bus station.
One month. My own key.
And if you leave?
You walk me to the road.
There's a job in Missoula in October. I'm not canceling it. I'm just looking at this first.
He came back. Nobody made him. I have no idea what to do with my hands.
What does Ronan do?
Give him a key. The only copy.
I work the spare off my ring. The only spare. I put it in his palm and fold his fingers over it.
You're not keeping a copy?
It's your door. I'll knock like anyone else.
Ronan gave Kai the only key to his room and kept no copy.
Offer the creek cabin. His own ground.
Not the bunkhouse. The cabin on the creek. Your own door, right on the line between us and nobody.
You're giving me the border.
I'm giving you the easiest exit on the mountain. On purpose.
Kai took a one-month trial in the creek cabin on the territory's edge, with his own key.
Say not yet. The Harlans are still angry.
Not this week. The Harlans are still angry. I won't invite you into a fight and call it a home.
That's my risk to weigh.
I hand him Silas's incident log instead of an argument. He reads it on the porch step.
Guest room. No key yet. Seven days, and then we talk again.
Ronan showed Kai the Harlan incident log; Kai chose seven days in the guest room with no key yet.
Dinner, If You Ask
Keep the trial terms real without assuming romance
Kai's doorway, Blackwood
Two weeks in, Friday, 6:45 PM
Two weeks in. Kai's door has a brass handle on the inside now. He checks it every time he walks in, like a guy patting his pocket for his wallet.
One month. Then I decide again.
And your own room.
No daily permission to go out.
No permission.
You can ask me to dinner.
Tonight?
I lean on the doorframe, my side of it. Ask properly, Alpha. Like you might hear no.
What does Ronan do?
Ask him properly. Mean the question.
Kai. Would you have dinner with me? Just us. You can say no, and I'll still make you a sandwich.
Yes. Obviously. But I'm picking the place.
He picks the diner at the county line, technically nobody's land. Ronan notices. He just smiles into his coffee.
Ronan asked Kai to dinner properly; Kai said yes and chose the diner on the county line.
Ask him to dinner as friends. Go slow.
Dinner. As friends. I want to learn how to be around you without trying to fix everything.
Friends is good. Friends is actually really good.
I shake his hand, which is ridiculous. We both hold on a second too long.
Ronan and Kai agreed to dinner as friends and to take things slow.
Don't ask. Keep this about the trial.
I'm not going to ask. Not while I'm the one who signs the rules you live under. That isn't fair to you.
I nod slowly. It stings. It's also the most respectful thing anyone has said to me on this mountain.
Then I'll eat with Silas. He makes terrible tea and says true things.
Ronan declined to ask Kai out while he held authority over the trial; Kai respected it and ate with Silas.
You Can Knock Again
Choose: stay by choice, a city life, or goodbye
The hallway outside Kai's room
Day thirty, 10:00 PM
Day thirty. The ledger has nineteen names in the Voluntary column and eleven blank lines where the claimed used to be.
The Harlans filed their objection. Then they signed. There are footnotes. I love footnotes.
I stand outside Kai's door. I could knock. I've been standing here four minutes, practicing the knock.
I open it before he does. My duffel is packed on the bed. The key is still on my ring.
I said I'd decide again tonight. So. Here's me, deciding.
Whatever he says, I walk him wherever he's going. That's the whole law now.
How does it end?
Knock anyway, and wait for his answer.
I close the door in his face. Gently. I hear him laugh on the other side. Then he knocks. Once. And waits.
I open it and step aside. The duffel gets unpacked. The key stays on my ring. The door stays mine.
Come in. And Ronan? You can knock again.
Kai chose to stay and invited Ronan into his room; the key and the door remain his.
Walk him to the bus. Ask for Saturdays.
Missoula. The job. I want a life that isn't the mountain's idea.
Then let me take you to dinner in your city. Any Saturday you say yes to. Nobody else's rules, not even mine.
Some Saturdays. Not all of them. And you ask every time.
Ronan walks him to the road, and this time past it, because this time he was invited.
Kai moved to Missoula for the job; he and Ronan agreed to non-exclusive Saturday dates, asked for every time.
Restore the old claim law. Keep the pack whole.
Three families will split off if the claim law stays dead. I'm bringing it back. For the pack.
Then I'm not staying under it.
I set the archive keys on the table. I'm going with him. Someone should write down what happened here honestly.
I walk them both to the road. It's the last law I still believe in. I stop at the line. Neither of them looks back.
Ronan restored the claim law to hold the pack together; Kai and Silas left, and Ronan lost both men's trust.
The Handle on the Inside
The exit right held, the Harlans signed, and the ledger became a list of people who asked to be there. Kai stayed because he chose to, with his own key, and invited Ronan in himself.
You can knock again.
Some Saturdays
Kai took the job in Missoula and a life that was nobody's idea but his. Ronan drives down on the Saturdays Kai says yes to, and asks every single time.
Ask me every time. I like being asked.
To the Road
Ronan kept the pack whole by bringing back the old law, and lost the two people who believed he wouldn't. He walked Kai and Silas to the road and stopped, exactly on the line.
To the road. Not past it.
